title: Integration Tests

writing.exampleCaption: The test imports `demo::answer` by crate name, as any outside caller would.
writing.explanation:
Files under `tests/` compile as separate crates and can only use the library's public API. That boundary catches accidental reliance on private implementation details.

An integration test behaves like an external user of your library. Each file under `tests/` is compiled as a separate crate and imports the public API by crate name. It cannot reach private helpers simply because they exist in the same repository. That constraint is valuable: if a test can accomplish a real task through the public interface, downstream callers probably can too.

The sample test imports `demo::answer` and asserts a stable result. Add a second test for a boundary case and a third for an error path. Give each a name that describes the promised behavior. Avoid testing private implementation details through elaborate scaffolding; those tests can become brittle when you refactor without changing the external contract. Unit tests next to the code are still useful for focused private logic. The two test locations serve different levels of confidence.

If an integration test needs a binary or fixture, make setup explicit and keep test cases independent so order does not matter. A test that relies on shared mutable files or network state can fail intermittently and hide real regressions. Run `cargo test --test public_api` while developing that file, then `cargo test` for the full suite. When a test fails, distinguish a library behavior change from a test assumption that was never part of the public contract. A small, representative collection of black-box tests often gives more confidence than many tests coupled to internal functions.
writing.feedback: A file under `tests/` is compiled as its own crate, so it sees only `pub` items, just as a downstream user would.

writing.success: The test passes through the public API, and you can say what it no longer depends on.

recall.question: Why prefer integration tests that use the public API over tests that reach internals through elaborate scaffolding?
recall.answer: Tests coupled to internals break when you refactor without changing the external contract. If a black-box test can do a real task through the public interface, downstream callers probably can too; private logic is better covered by unit tests beside the code.

recall.question: Why are integration tests that share mutable files or network state risky, and what is the remedy?
recall.answer: They can pass or fail depending on run order or the environment, so they fail intermittently and hide real regressions. Make setup explicit and keep each test independent so order does not matter.
